R06-F-01: For most of its history the word 'computer' named an occupation rather than a machine. Observatories, survey offices and, later, engineering firms employed rooms of people whose work consisted of carrying out long calculations, often for tables of positions, tides or trajectories that others would use. It is tempting to treat these workers as a quaint prelude to the real story, a stopgap that lasted only until electronics arrived. That reading gets the relation backwards. The electronic computer did not introduce the idea of mechanical calculation into a world that lacked it; it inherited an idea that human computing offices had already worked out in detail. The key feature of such offices was not the arithmetic skill of any individual but the way the work was organised. A planner with mathematical training would break a difficult problem into a sequence of simple steps, write those steps on printed sheets, and hand the sheets to workers who needed to know only how to add, subtract and look up values in a table. The workers did not have to understand why a step was there, and the scheme was in fact designed so that they would not need to. Errors were caught not by insight but by procedure: two people would compute the same column independently, and any disagreement sent the column back. What was being built, in effect, was a method in which correctness no longer depended on anyone grasping the whole. Seen this way, much of what we think of as distinctive about programming was already present. The separation between the person who designs a procedure and the agent who executes it, the reduction of judgement to rules, the checking of results by redundancy rather than by understanding: all of these were practices before they were properties of machines. When the first electronic machines were built, their designers could borrow not only mathematical techniques from the computing offices but also a whole conception of what it meant to make a calculation reliable. None of this is to say that the machines merely did faster what people had done slowly. Speed of the magnitude electronics provided changed which problems were worth posing at all; calculations that would have occupied a room of workers for years became routine, and whole fields grew up around them. But the continuity matters, because it reminds us that the habit of treating thought as something that can be divided, written down and handed to an executor who need not understand it is a social invention before it is a technical one. Its consequences, good and bad, were visible in offices long before they were visible on screens.
R06-F-02: The most familiar complaint about recommendation algorithms is that they trap each of us in a private enclosure. Because a system learns what a user has clicked, watched or bought, the argument runs, it will keep offering more of the same, until every listener hears only the music that confirms their existing taste and every reader meets only the opinions they already hold. On this picture the danger is fragmentation: a public that once shared a common stock of songs, books and news splinters into millions of sealed niches, each tuned to one person. The complaint is not baseless, but it may have the main tendency of these systems the wrong way round. Most recommendation engines do not learn from one user in isolation; they learn from the aggregate behaviour of very large numbers of users, and they rank items partly by how much engagement those items have already attracted. That design creates a feedback loop. An item that gets a slight early lead is shown to more people, which earns it more engagement, which earns it still more prominence. Imagine two songs of equal appeal released on the same day, one of which happens to be picked up by a few enthusiastic listeners in its first hours. Under such a loop the small, accidental difference can harden into an enormous gap, and the second song may effectively disappear, not because anyone judged it worse but because no one was shown it. If this is right, the characteristic risk is less fragmentation than concentration: attention pooling ever more heavily on a few items, while the vast catalogue that digital distribution made available sits largely unvisited. The early hope that online platforms would let obscure work find its small audiences depended on people actually encountering that work, and a ranking system that rewards prior popularity makes such encounters rarer than the size of the catalogue suggests. It would be wrong to present this as something algorithms invented. Bestseller lists, radio playlists and the front tables of bookshops have always amplified what was already selling, and cultural markets have long been marked by a few large successes and many neglected works. What is new is the speed of the loop and its invisibility. A bookseller choosing what to display is a person whose choices can be questioned; a ranking produced by continuous automated feedback appears simply to report what people want, when it is partly manufacturing it. The remedy, if there is one, lies less in protecting users from their own tastes than in asking how much of what looks like popular demand is an echo of earlier exposure.
R06-F-03: Debates about privacy in the age of large data sets usually begin from an image of ownership. Each person, on this view, holds a store of information about themselves, and the moral question is whether that information is taken with or without their permission. Hence the enormous weight placed on consent: the checkbox, the privacy notice, the setting that lets a user decline to share. If people are told what will happen to their data and agree to it, the transaction is treated as legitimate, and if they refuse, they are thought to have protected themselves. The difficulty is that much personal information is not individual in the way the image assumes. A person who uploads their contact list discloses the names and numbers of people who agreed to nothing. Someone who submits a sample to a genetic testing service reveals facts about parents, siblings and cousins, some of whom may not know the test was taken. More subtly, when enough people share information about their habits, a system can learn the patterns that link one trait to another, and then infer those traits in people who shared nothing at all. A person who declines to disclose, say, a health condition may find that it has been estimated, with fair accuracy, from purchases and movements that resemble those of people who did disclose it. One might reply that the refuser has still kept their own data, and that what others choose to reveal is their own affair. But this misses what the refuser was trying to protect. Nobody declines to share a fact for the sake of a particular row in a database; they decline because they do not want the fact known. If it can be known anyway, through the choices of others, then the refusal has secured very little, and the consent framework, which places the whole burden of protection on individual decisions, has quietly ceased to describe what is actually happening. This does not make individual consent worthless. Being asked still matters, and a person who is deceived about how their information will be used has been wronged in a way that the collective character of data does not erase. The point is that consent cannot carry the load it has been given. Privacy behaves in part like clean air or quiet streets: a condition that each person's conduct affects for others, and that no one can secure for themselves by private choice alone. Protecting it therefore requires rules about what may be inferred and done, not merely about who has clicked agree.
R06-F-04: When an automated system fails and a human operator fails to rescue it, the official account usually ends with the words 'human error'. The phrase is accurate in a narrow sense, since a person did do the wrong thing, but it hides the way the situation was produced. Automation is typically introduced to take over the parts of a task that are routine and well understood. What remains for the human is whatever the designers could not automate: the rare, ambiguous, fast-moving situations in which the machine gives up or behaves strangely. The person is thus left with the hardest part of the job, and is expected to perform it suddenly, after long periods of doing almost nothing. Those long periods matter. Skill at controlling a process is kept alive by exercising it, and an operator who has spent months watching a screen rather than flying, steering or adjusting will have less of it than one who did the work by hand. Worse, the automation removes the everyday experience through which people build an intuitive model of how the system behaves, so that when something goes wrong they must reason about it from first principles, under pressure, with alarms sounding. Monitoring is also something human beings do badly. Attention drifts when nothing happens for hours, and the more reliable the machine, the longer the stretches in which nothing happens. The result is a curious inversion. The better the automation works in ordinary conditions, the less prepared its human supervisors may be for the extraordinary ones, and the more surprising their failure will look when it comes. Calling that failure human error locates the fault in the individual at the very moment when the design of the whole arrangement deserves scrutiny. None of this is a case against automation, which has removed a great deal of tedium and many kinds of mistake. It is a case for designing automated systems around the people who must step in when they fail. That might mean having operators run the process manually at regular intervals so that their skill does not decay, building displays that show what the machine is doing and why rather than only whether it is working, or deciding deliberately that some tasks should remain shared even when they could be fully automated. Such measures cost efficiency in the short run. Their justification is that the moments they prepare for, although rare, are the ones in which the most is at stake.
R06-F-05: Few technical metaphors have succeeded as completely as the cloud. To store files 'in the cloud' is to imagine them floating somewhere overhead, available from anywhere, belonging to no place in particular and weighing nothing at all. The image is not simply wrong; from the point of view of a user, it describes the experience rather well. A photograph taken on a phone appears on a laptop moments later, and the user neither knows nor needs to know where it has been in between. Yet the metaphor has migrated from describing an experience to shaping how whole societies think about a vast industrial system, and in that second role it misleads. What sits behind the cloud is emphatically material. It consists of large buildings filled with servers, which consume great quantities of electricity and must be kept cool, often with water drawn from local supplies; of cables laid across sea floors and along railway lines; of particular sites chosen for cheap power, favourable taxes or stable ground. Each of these is somewhere, and being somewhere means being subject to the laws of a particular state, to the weather and geology of a particular region, and to the politics of the towns asked to host the buildings and supply their power. A data centre can strain a local grid or compete with farms for water, and a damaged cable can slow communication across a region. The metaphor makes all of this hard to see. A cloud has no address, so questions about which country's courts can demand access to stored data come to seem technical rather than political. A cloud uses nothing, so the energy cost of keeping old files indefinitely available is easy to forget. And a cloud is diffuse, which suggests resilience, whereas in practice a large share of the services people rely on may depend on a small number of companies and sites, so that a single failure can ripple outward with surprising speed. Defenders of the metaphor might point out that hiding complexity is precisely what good computing does. Nobody wants to think about the location of a server before sending a message, and abstractions of this kind are why ordinary people can use powerful systems at all. That is true, but it confuses two audiences. Abstraction is a gift to the user at the moment of use; it becomes a liability when it is carried over into the deliberations of citizens, regulators and planners, whose task is precisely to decide where the buildings go, who supplies their power and whose laws govern what they hold. For them, the useful question is not where the cloud is but how it came to seem to be nowhere.
R06-F-06: Whenever a machine produces fluent language, the question returns of whether it understands what it says. Two answers dominate. One holds that understanding is shown in behaviour: if a system answers questions, follows instructions and sustains a conversation in ways we cannot distinguish from a competent person, there is nothing further we could reasonably ask of it, and to withhold the word is mere prejudice in favour of our own kind. The other holds that behaviour, however impressive, can be produced by manipulating symbols whose connection to the world the system never grasps, and that understanding requires something behind the performance, some grounding of words in perception, action or experience. The two camps disagree about almost everything except one assumption, and that shared assumption is where the trouble lies. Both treat understanding as a single property that a system either has or lacks, so that the only task is to decide which side of the line it falls on. Yet when we attribute understanding to people we do nothing of the kind. A student may understand a theorem well enough to apply it to textbook problems but not well enough to see why it fails when one condition is dropped; a mechanic may understand an engine thoroughly in practice while being unable to explain its thermodynamics. We judge understanding by a battery of loosely connected abilities: explaining, extending to unfamiliar cases, noticing one's own mistakes, connecting what one knows to what one does. These abilities can come apart, and people possess them in very different measures. If understanding is a cluster of this kind, the all-or-nothing question about machines is badly posed. A system may display some of the abilities to a high degree and others hardly at all; it may extend a pattern brilliantly in one domain and fail, without any sign of noticing, at a trivial variation in another. Saying that it 'really understands' flattens this profile into a verdict that tells us little, and saying that it 'merely manipulates symbols' does the same in the opposite direction. The useful work lies in mapping which abilities are present, under what conditions, and how robustly. This proposal will not satisfy everyone. Someone who believes that understanding involves an inner experience of meaning will say that mapping abilities, however finely, leaves the essential question untouched. Perhaps it does. But that question, whatever its answer, is a question about experience, and it arises equally for any being whose inner life we cannot inspect. It should not be allowed to stand in for the more tractable question of what a system can and cannot reliably do, which is, after all, the question on which most practical decisions about such systems depend.
R06-F-07: Suppose a lender uses a scoring system to estimate how likely each applicant is to default, and suppose applicants belong to two groups that differ, for whatever historical reasons, in how often their members in fact default. There are several natural ways to ask whether the system treats the groups fairly. One may ask whether a given score means the same thing in both groups, so that among applicants scored as having a one-in-five chance of default, roughly one in five defaults whichever group they belong to. One may ask instead whether applicants who would in fact have repaid are wrongly refused at the same rate in both groups, or whether those who would in fact have defaulted are wrongly approved at the same rate. Each of these looks like a reasonable requirement, and each has been proposed as the meaning of fairness. It turns out that they cannot, in general, all be satisfied together. When the groups' underlying default rates differ and the prediction is less than perfect, a score that means the same thing in both groups will produce different rates of error between them, in wrongful refusals, wrongful approvals or both, and equalising both kinds of error will make the same score mean different things in different groups. This is not a defect of any particular system that better engineering might remove; it follows from the arithmetic of prediction under unequal base rates. The finding was greeted in some quarters as a kind of scandal, and two conclusions were quickly drawn from it: that the idea of a fair algorithm is incoherent, or, conversely, that since some criterion must be chosen, the choice is a technical matter best left to the people who build the systems. Both conclusions seem to me mistaken, and for related reasons. The impossibility does not show that fairness is incoherent; it shows that our everyday notion of fairness bundles together several demands that usually travel together and part company only under specific conditions. Discovering that two values can conflict is not the same as discovering that one of them is empty, any more than the occasional conflict between honesty and kindness shows that one of these is an illusion. Nor does the need to choose make the choice technical. Which criterion should give way depends on what the decision does to the people it touches: who bears the cost of being wrongly refused, how severe that cost is, and whether the different base rates are themselves the residue of earlier unfairness that the decision would perpetuate. Those are questions about harm and responsibility, not about arithmetic. It is worth adding that the dilemma is not peculiar to algorithms. A loan officer who judges applicants by experience faces exactly the same trade-off whenever the groups differ in base rates; the officer simply does not have to declare which criterion is being sacrificed, and may not know. In this respect the formal analysis has done something valuable. By making the conflict explicit, it has turned a choice that was always being made silently into one that must be made in the open, and has removed the comfortable belief that a sufficiently careful decision maker could satisfy every reasonable demand at once. The danger is that the explicitness is squandered, that the choice is buried again inside the system, this time under a layer of technical vocabulary instead of a layer of personal discretion.
R06-F-08: Two complaints about digital information circulate side by side, and at first sight they cannot both be true. The first is that the internet never forgets: an embarrassing photograph or an ill-judged remark, once posted, may resurface years later, copied onto sites its author has never heard of. The second is that digital records are alarmingly fragile: web pages vanish, links lead nowhere, and files saved in formats that no current program can read become, for practical purposes, meaningless strings of bits. One might expect a medium to be either durable or perishable, and it is puzzling to hear the same medium accused of both. The puzzle dissolves once we stop asking about the medium and start asking about copying. A single digital copy is, if anything, more perishable than a sheet of paper. Paper survives neglect; a letter left in a drawer can usually be read a century later by anyone who knows the language. A file left on an old disk depends on the disk surviving, on a machine that can still read the disk, and on software that can still interpret the file, and each of these dependencies decays on its own schedule. What digital information has, and paper largely lacks, is the capacity to be copied perfectly, instantly and at almost no cost. Its persistence therefore depends far less on the durability of any one copy than on whether enough people, or enough systems, have reasons to keep making copies. Seen in this light, the two complaints describe the same mechanism working on different material. The embarrassing photograph persists because it is the kind of thing people want to pass on, so it is duplicated faster than any single copy can be deleted. The municipal report, the small society's newsletter and the scholar's personal website persist only as long as someone pays for the server and remembers to renew the domain, because few people have any reason to copy them. Nothing about these documents makes them harder to store than the photograph; a newsletter occupies less space than most images. What they lack is a constituency of copiers. When the society disbands or the scholar retires, the single copy that existed sits on a server whose bills no one is paying, and one day it is simply gone, often without anyone noticing that it has happened. Digital persistence, in short, tracks attention and interest rather than value, and the material most likely to vanish is often the unglamorous record that matters most to a historian a generation later. This suggests that preservation in a digital age is less a technical problem than an institutional one. Better storage media help, but no medium keeps information alive by itself; what keeps it alive is an organisation that has made copying it someone's duty, and that will go on paying for that duty when the material has ceased to be interesting. Libraries and archives have long performed this role for print, and some are trying to perform it for the web. It is tempting to hope that automated tools, which can gather enormous quantities of web pages without human effort, have made such institutions unnecessary. They have not: what such tools gather must still be stored, checked and kept readable as formats change, and someone must decide what deserves that continuing expense. Archives face a difficulty that print archives faced less acutely: the sheer volume of material means that they must choose, and every choice about what to copy is also, in effect, a choice about what to let disappear. The task cannot be avoided by declaring that everything is saved, because what is left to the accidents of attention is saved very unevenly.
